title: 40 years apart. Two messages. One unmissable piece of guidance.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton sets two pieces of advice side by side, forty years apart. In the 1980s, school-improvement researcher Joseph Murphy found that more effective schools had a focus on learning and high levels of consistency. In 2026, the head of Bishopshalt School, rated exceptional in every category in England's new inspection round, names a mantra that tomorrow will be better than today and a relentless consistency. He reads this as confirmation of the foundations of his own Looking for Learning series. The argument turns on a paradox: the recipe is simple and already known, yet it cannot be created quickly or alone, and it demands negotiated agreement on what is shared and what is left to individuals. He closes with questions for leaders to ask of their own school or classroom.
points: Two independent sources four decades apart point to the same pair of qualities: a total focus on learning and relentless consistency.
There is no secret to an exceptional school; the difficulty lies in the sustained time, leadership and community commitment needed to apply what is already known.
Rapid turnaround changes tend to stay on the surface, so both focus and consistency have to be built with stakeholders over time.
Consistency has to be negotiated, with the community agreeing what everyone signs up to and where individuals stay free.
quotes: But in one way, Bishopshalt is anything but average. It is one of very few schools in the UK to have been considered ‘exceptional’ in all eight of the criteria of the new inspection framework.
I doubt that this is a result of the UK inspection programme. More likely, the inspection programme has found and made public the evidence of a school that is doing exceptionally well.

With 30 or 40 years between them, Joseph Murphy and Liam McGillicuddy give us the same advice if we want our classrooms and schools to become really good. It’s all about a total focus on learning across all aspects of the school - tomorrow will be better than today - and a relentless focus on consistency.

Blend together a deep focus on getting better and a high level of consistency across your school, classroom and organisation and you have a very good chance of reaching high levels of effectiveness. Both of these characteristics have been a feature in every good or very good school I have ever seen.

You can’t create a deep focus on getting better (learning) and high levels of consistency over a short period of time. Or, if you do, as we saw in the Substack about turnaround schools, those changes often don’t take root but remain on the surface.

But it takes rigorous focus and commitment to get there. It takes time. It takes consistent, thoughtful leadership and management to hold people’s feet to the fire and it takes a fully-focused community who resolve not to let each other down by being individualistic where it is unhelpful.
